extracted.intended_audience: Presbyterian ministers, church office-bearers, and laity concerned with church polity and reformation principles in 18th-century Scotland
extracted.subtask_description: A formal presbytery testimony enumerating grievances and standards by which the Revolution Church and state conduct are condemned — covering Erastian encroachments, civil impositions, union with England, toleration, tyranny, discipline, and doctrinal unfaithfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of Erastian supremacy (civil headship over church)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever pertains to solemnities is entrusted to, and required of, the ministers of the Lord, without the intervention of civil authority; the church's head (Christ) committed the power of the keys to ecclesiastical officers, not to civil rulers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The testimony repeatedly asserts that spiritual supremacy exercised by the state over ecclesiastical matters (Erastianism) is a usurpation of Christ's headship. Scriptural citations invoked include Matth. xvi.19, xviii.18; John xx.23. The church must refuse taking instructions about worship or ministerial functions from any head other than Christ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilly-appointed national fasts are improper
rubrics_metrics.description: National fasts appointed by civil authorities (often on account of wars) and enforced with civil pains are improper because they make ministers observe fasts 'the professed design of which includes success to the interest of the avowed enemies of our glorious Redeemer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such fasts are condemned because they subordinate the solemnity of fasting to the arbitrament of civil powers; ministers are the proper parties to appoint and observe fasts, not magistrates. The practice is described as 'a base subjection of the worship of God' and an example of Erastianism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil imposition of acts/oaths on ministers under ecclesiastical pains
rubrics_metrics.description: The king and parliament arbitrarily imposing acts and statutes upon ministers and preachers under ecclesiastical pains and censures (e.g. acts requiring oaths of allegiance/assurance/abjuration) is a sinful Erastian encroachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific statutory examples cited: Act 6th, 1706; Act 1707; acts in George I's reign requiring oaths and public prayer for the monarch, and prescribing forms of prayer for the Church of Scotland. The practice amounts to civil power modeling worship and doctrine and using ecclesiastical censures as penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers should not be compelled to read civil statutes in divine service
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring ministers to read civil acts (e.g. the Act framed after Captain Porteous's murder to be read in every parish church) in divine service profanes the Lord's day and corrupts worship by 'immixing human inventions' with divine worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Porteous Act (1737) is cited: ministers ordered to read it on the Lord's day under ecclesiastical penalties, failing which they could be deprived of voting or even of ecclesiastical benefices. Such impositions are characterized as framing mischief into law and an Erastian practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to patronage and civil selection of ministers
rubrics_metrics.description: Patronage — restoration of patrons' rights to present ministers and exclusion of the people from a vote in calling their ministers — is an Erastian usurpation, anti-christian, without warrant in Scripture or apostolic practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The testimony traces patronage's restoration (acts of 1690 and 1712) and criticizes the church for embracing and confirming patrons' powers by acts of assembly. Patronage is called an 'intolerable yoke' and contrary to Acts i, 15-24; vi,2-7; xiv,23; xvi,9 and apostolic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of the incorporating union with England
rubrics_metrics.description: The incorporating union with England is condemned as founded on violation of the Solemn League and Covenant and as destructive of the formerly attained uniformity in religion between nations; it obliges Scotland to support the idolatrous Church of England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The union is criticized for engrossing the English act establishing Prelacy into Scottish law and for annulling prior covenanted acts. The union's articles (and the English act securing Church of England hierarchy) are used to show the union legally entrenches Prelacy and prevents a revival of covenanted reformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imposition of oaths contradictory to Presbyterian principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The imposition of oaths (notably the oath of abjuration and other allegiance oaths) that bind subjects to acknowledge the prelatic Erastian constitution and the union are sinful and at variance with the oath of the covenants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The testimony clarifies that the objection is doctrinal and constitutional, not merely political — the oaths compel maintenance of Prelacy and the Church of England as by law established. The act of limitation referenced makes the oath explicitly intended to secure the Church of England and the present constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to broad toleration that protects prelatical worship and open sects
rubrics_metrics.description: The toleration act (anno 1712) that protects Episcopal communion and opens a wide door to sects and heretics undermines true religion and removes civil support for church discipline (e.g., civil pains of excommunication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toleration is presented as 'the most effectual method that ever the policy of hell hatched' to destroy true religion. The act permits Episcopal clergy to administer ordinances with popish canons; it withdraws civil concurrence for church discipline and thus undermines Presbyterian government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of tyranny and arbitrary civil practices affecting conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: The civil powers' tyranny — fining, imprisoning, dispensing with divine law (e.g., pardons, reprieves, repeal of penal statutes against witches) — and the church's collusion or imitation of such arbitrary measures are condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: imprisonments for conscience (refusal to swear fidelity), pardons like Porteous's, the 1735 act repealing penal statutes against witchcraft, and oppressive taxation to support pensioners and wars are cited as contradictions of divine law and evidence of tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to arbitrary and partisan church government (tyranny in church discipline)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Revolution Church's arbitrary prosecutions, suspensions, depositions, and collaboration with civil magistrates against faithful ministers who protested defections (e.g., John Hepburn, Gilchrist, Taylor, McMillan, McNeil) demonstrate tyrannical government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The testimony recounts prosecutions leading to suspension, deposition, imprisonment, and being proclaimed rebels for those pleading for covenanted reformation. The assembly's commission empowered to censure and to apply to civil magistrates to suppress dissent is singled out as tyrannical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to partiality and laxity in discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The church is guilty of partiality: strict censures fall on faithful reformers, while the loose, profane, and erroneous (often the rich) escape censure; gross scandals (drunkenness, blasphemy, sabbath-breaking, uncleanness) are often overlooked, and offenders admitted to sacraments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The testimony condemns selling censures for money, overlooking rich offenders, admitting those guilty of gross sins to office and sacraments, tolerating heretical teachers, and failing to purge the house of God. This partiality is contrasted with the expected faithful exercise of church discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfaithfulness in doctrine and failure to vindicate Presbyterian principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The church has not formally declared Christ as sole king and supreme head of the church nor affirmed the divine right of presbytery and condemned other forms; it has exhibited doctrinal unsoundness (e.g., condemning the Marrow of Modern Divinity and encouraging Baxterian principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of doctrinal unfaithfulness include the church's condemnation of The Marrow (seen as denying gospel truths), toleration of Arminian/Pelagian/Arian teachings, and failure to inflict adequate censures on professors (cases of Mr. Simpson, Mr. Campbell, Mr. Glas) who taught doctrines judged heretical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to properly censure and remove heretical teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: When ministers or professors were convicted of gross errors (e.g., Simpson's Arminian/Socinian/Arian errors; Campbell's dangerous principles; Glas's renunciation of presbytery), the church often dismissed or leniently admonished them rather than imposing adequate censure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The testimony details the Simpson case (dismissed with gentle admonition despite denial of Christ's necessary existence and other errors), the Campbell case (published principles subverting revealed religion), and Glas (advocating independent schemes), to illustrate institutional lenity toward doctrinal corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to forced intrusions of ministers into vacant congregations
rubrics_metrics.description: Violent intrusions of ministers into vacant churches over the will of the people, followed by excommunication of those who refuse to submit to intruders, are condemned as magisterial and lordly power exercised over the flock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such intrusions are described as exemplars of the church's arbitrary government; those who conscientiously reject intruded ministers are excommunicated from sealing ordinances, while proponents of intrusion face little censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of cultural profanities tolerated by the church (e.g., stage plays)
rubrics_metrics.description: The church's toleration or even encouragement of play-houses, stage players, and theatrical entertainments (including a minister authoring a profane play) is condemned as promoting immorality and exposing what is sacred to ridicule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play-houses in principal cities, stage players among the most abandoned, and a minister authoring 'The Tragedy of Douglas' are cited as examples. The testimony views such entertainments as 'seminaries of vice and impiety' and incompatible with faithful church conduct.
